If I had to pick one thread that keeps appearing in the literature, it’s consistency. Not perfection, just showing up for your body day after day with enough sleep, regular movement, and food that actually nourishes you rather than just fills you up. It’s not particularly glamorous, but it’s what the evidence keeps pointing to as the foundation everything else rests on. Stress management and social connection tend to show up right alongside it, because health isn’t just physical—it’s deeply tied to how we live and who we’re around.

That said, health is highly individual. What works for one person might not work for another, and underlying conditions, medications, work schedules, and even your neighbourhood all play a role. If you’d like to look into it properly, I’d be glad to pull together some of the best-reviewed resources we have. Our reference collection has excellent, clearly written primers from the Mayo Clinic, the NHS, and the CDC, and we also subscribe to a couple of health databases that let you search peer-reviewed articles without hitting a paywall.

I shall be plain with you, sir: the very first and most indispensable duty is to secure clean air. Nothing else compares. When the lungs draw in a pure atmosphere, the blood runs clear, the humours keep their natural balance, and the constitution stands firm against whatever ill may be abroad. But let a man breathe the stagnant vapours of a neglected court, the sour breath of an overflowing midden, or the damp exhalations of an ill-drained cellar, and you may be certain the fever will follow. I have watched whole families laid low in a single week when the cesspool ran back into the yard, and I have seen them rise again within ten days when the drains were cleared and the windows opened to the morning breeze.

Therefore, whatever your station, attend to the air you breathe. Sweep the yards, empty the privies, pave the ground so it does not hold water, and let every room be aired thoroughly before nightfall. Keep the damp from your walls, avoid the heavy night air, and never suffer a child to sleep in a cellar or a garret that smells of rot. Tonics and pills may support a weakened frame, but they cannot undo the work of foul air. Cleanliness, drainage, and ventilation—these are the true physicians. All else is but dressing the wound while the poison still enters the blood.

It was during the autumn of '47, during the second visitation of the cholera. I was called to a cellar in Back Lane, where the ground was perpetually wet and the windows mere slits choked with soot. A young mother lay upon a straw mattress, and beside her, a child of perhaps six years, seized with the cramp and the collapse.

The air in that room was heavy, sir; it had a weight to it, a visible yellowish tinge that clung to the throat. I could smell the stagnant water from the privy below, the rot of the coal, the sweat of six persons living in a space meant for two. I did all that science permits: I applied mustard plasters to the abdomen, I gave calomel to purge the bowels, and I ordered the windows thrown open, though the cold was biting. I even burned a bowl of sulphur to purify the atmosphere.

But the child did not recover. By the morning, she was gone. The mother followed three days later.

I still think of that day because I knew, with every fibre of my being, that my medicine was not at fault. The poison was not in the blood alone, but in the very air she breathed. I stood in that doorway and told the landlord that unless that cellar was drained and ventilated, the next family would die in the same way. He told me of rent and of repairs. I tell you this because I have never been able to forget the smell of that room. It is a reminder that while I can treat the symptom, I cannot cure the cause without the help of the state. That is why I fight for the drains.
